title: Why standing
hook: the Ardas is said standing: readiness and respect, like standing before a king

segments.voice: Yesterday, shukrana: joy gets an Ardas too, a thank-you with nothing added. Today, not the words of the Ardas but the body that says them.

A judge walks into a courtroom and everyone rises. A national anthem starts and a stadium stands up, even the people holding nachos. In some classrooms, a teacher walks in and the whole room gets to its feet. Standing is an old way of saying: this matters, and I'm paying attention. In the gurdwara, when it's time for the Ardas, the whole congregation stands. Hands are folded. Faces turn toward the Guru Granth Sahib. Nobody needs to be told why.
screen: `ALL RISE.` → `A STADIUM ON ITS FEET.` → `THE CONGREGATION STANDS.`

segments.voice: The Ardas is often called the standing prayer, and Sikhs give a few reasons for the posture that fit together. The first is respect. Sikhs speak of the Guru as the true king, sacha paatshah. The picture is a royal court, where a petition was presented standing, hands joined, and the Ardas, a petition, is made the same way before the Guru Granth Sahib. The second is readiness. Someone sitting is resting; someone standing can move. Sikh history remembers people who stood up for others, and the posture keeps that in the body: whatever is asked for, the one asking is ready to act on it. The third is togetherness. When everyone stands, nobody is above anyone else. The grandmother and the teenager, the regular and the first-time visitor, are on their feet side by side. Just before the Ardas, a line from Sukhmani Sahib, on ang 268, is often recited. It says, in effect: You are the Master, to You is this prayer; body and soul are all Your gift. It sets the tone: not a list of demands, but servants presenting themselves. And one thing, plainly. The posture is a custom of respect, not a test. People who can't stand, the elderly, the sick, someone with a baby asleep on their lap, join the Ardas sitting, and they're no less part of it. Standing is what the heart is doing. The legs just help when they can.
screen: `RESPECT: BEFORE THE TRUE KING.` · `READINESS: READY TO ACT.` · `TOGETHERNESS: NOBODY ABOVE.` · `ANG 268: YOU ARE THE MASTER.` · then, large: `STAND READY.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand up now, feet a little apart, hands folded in front of your chest if you like; if you can't stand, sit up tall and let your spine do the standing. Notice whether it feels different from sitting: more awake, maybe, or more ready. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, standing, and let that be your whole prayer for now.
Why standing. The Ardas is said standing, hands joined: respect before the true king, readiness to act, and everyone equal on their feet.
Your line: stand ready. Respect, readiness, and nobody above anyone else. Day six hundred forty-three, counted.

howItsDone: Sikhs stand for the Ardas with hands joined, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, often after reciting 'tu thakur tum peh ardaas' from Sukhmani Sahib; those who cannot stand join seated.

Standing makes the prayer valid, so sitting means you haven't really joined in.
It's so people can leave the moment the Ardas is finished.
